Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Use only the examples on the slides; nobody shares a real chat. Take any real incident, threat, or shared image to a counselor or dean that day.

Every student in the room

When the Theo card comes up, note that a leaked screenshot can out someone, and remember that short or literal replies may come from a student writing in a second language or reading tone differently.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open plainly: “Nobody shares a real chat today. This is about the minute after your stomach drops.”

Slide 2 · Notes

Everyone votes at once with a fist or up to five fingers. The room splits; that’s the point. Ask: “What would you need to know to be sure?”

Slide 3 · Notes

Ask: “Where were you the last time you sent a one-word reply?” Practice, driving, babysitting, half asleep.

Slide 4 · Notes

Ask: “Ever been sure someone was mad, and they weren’t?” Most hands go up silently. That’s the gap.

Slide 5 · Notes

Let it sit. Ask: “If you’re only right two times in three, what’s the smart move before you react?”

Slide 6 · Notes

Ask: “Which one do you skip most?” Usually number one.

Slide 7 · Notes

2 to 3 minutes in pairs. “They’re mad” is allowed as one read, just not the only one. Ask for a reply that checks it out.

Slide 8 · Notes

Private. Think of a reply you almost sent once. Run it through. Then: “Not replying is a reply. So is ‘let me think about it.’”

Slide 9 · Notes

Groups talk, report back; the next slide shows the point. Dani’s dad works Saturdays, so it matters. Asking again by name is fine.

Slide 10 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 11 · Notes

Groups talk, report back; the next slide shows the point. Not every chat has to include you. If she raises it: “not trying to make it a thing, it just stung.”

Slide 12 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 13 · Notes

Groups talk, report back; the next slide shows the point. Keep the talk off who Theo likes.

Slide 14 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 15 · Notes

Ask: “Why is not replying so hard in the moment?”

Slide 16 · Notes

Ask: “Who’s the one person you’d want messaging you if it were you?” Be that.

Slide 17 · Notes

Ask: “What’s something about how you text that people outside your family might not get?” For you, or people you know.

Slide 18 · Notes

Turn and talk. Then ask: “Where else in your life does this show up?” Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 19 · Notes

Let them answer in their heads or on a card they keep. Share the take-home link after: the three reads, the screenshot test, who to talk to.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why text misleads (tone is stripped out and our mood fills it in), use the read-it-three-ways steps and the screenshot test before replying, and name one move for when a chat turns on someone. Nobody shares a real chat.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 4 minWhat does “ok.” mean? (fist to five)
  2. 8 minWhat text deletes, what your brain adds, the tone gap
  3. 8 minRead it three ways (pairs), then the screenshot test
  4. 8 minThree moments, one per slide
  5. 6 minWhen a pile-on starts: if it’s you, if you’re watching
  6. 6 minEvery student in the room, where else this shows up, and the close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The “ok.” vote, read it three ways, one of the three moments, the pile-on slides, and the close. Share the take-home link afterward.

Before you teach
No real chats, no real names.

Use only the examples on the slides. Don't ask students to show their phones, read real messages, or describe a fight they're in. Someone in the room may be the target of a chat right now, and someone may have been part of a pile-on.

If a real incident comes up, take it out of the room.

If a student names an ongoing situation, thank them, say you want to help with it privately, and move on. Follow up that day with a counselor or dean.

Know which chats need an adult right away.

Threats to hurt someone or talk about a weapon. Someone saying they want to hurt themselves or die, even as a "joke." The same person targeted again and again. Don't ask about these in class. Any disclosure goes to a counselor the same day.

Sexual images of anyone under 18.

Students may mention nudes or AI-made images. Say calmly: don't forward, don't save, tell an adult. Don't ask to see anything. In Massachusetts, sharing a sexual image of someone under 18 can bring legal consequences even between teens, and a 2024 law made sharing anyone's intimate images without consent, including deepfakes, a crime.

Telling an adult will feel like snitching to some students.

Name the worry out loud. Frame telling as looking out for someone, and say plainly what happens next at your school when a student reports a chat.

Leave room for the student who joined in.

Some students have forwarded or laughed at something they regret. Give them a way back: stop adding, delete what you can, and apologize directly without excuses. Keep shame out of it so they can use it.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

People raise hurt in different ways.

Some students say it straight out. Others show it by spending time elsewhere, depending on family, culture, and the friendship. Present both as normal and ask students what fits them and what this friend will actually hear.

A leaked message can out someone.

The Theo scenario says "someone he likes" on purpose. A screenshot that reveals who a student likes, or their gender identity, can put them at risk at school or at home. Treat that as a same-day counselor conversation, never a discussion topic.

Reading tone is harder for some students.

Autistic students, students with ADHD, and students with social anxiety may misread or overthink texts more, or reply in short, literal ways that others misread. "Ask instead of guessing" helps everyone. Don't make fast replies or emoji a sign of being a good friend.

English may be a second language in the chat.

Some students text in English as a second language or switch between languages, and short or plain replies may be how they write. Add that to "read it as if they're busy" as another reason a reply can look cold.

Not every student has their own phone.

Some share a family phone, have limited data, or have phone limits for family or faith reasons, and may miss chats for those reasons alone. The moves work for any group, online or in person, and mute, read receipts, and focus modes are free.

"Tell an adult" means any adult they trust.

That could be a parent or caregiver, a grandparent, an older cousin, a coach, a teacher, or a counselor. Not every student can bring this home, so always name a school adult too.

What the research says

People sending and reading short messages were about 89% sure they'd read the tone right. Face to face they were right about three times in four; over email, less than two in three. Senders were just as overconfident.

Kruger, Epley, Parker and Ng, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2005

The overconfidence comes from egocentrism: you hear your own voice in your head as you type, so it's hard to imagine the message reading any other way.

Kruger et al., 2005

One-word text replies like "Okay." read as less sincere with a period than without one. The same replies on handwritten notes showed no difference.

Gunraj et al., Computers in Human Behavior, 2016 (Binghamton University)

In the Cyberball studies, more than 1,400 people from 62 countries reported a drop in belonging and mood when two strangers stopped throwing them a ball in an online game.

Williams, Cheung and Choi, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2000

The more people in an online chat room, the longer it took someone asking for help to get it. When the request named a specific person, the delay nearly disappeared.

Markey, Computers in Human Behavior, 2000

46% of U.S. teens ages 13 to 17 had experienced at least one of six kinds of online harassment, most often offensive name-calling. Among girls 15 to 17, it was 54%.

Pew Research Center, Teens and Cyberbullying, 2022

A 2024 law added an education-based diversion program for teens who share sexual images of minors, and made sharing anyone's intimate images without consent, including AI deepfakes, a crime.

Massachusetts, An Act to prevent abuse and exploitation (H.4744), 2024
